translations.text: The martyrdom of Miles, bishop of Susa, and of Aborsam the priest and Sinai the deacon, at the beginning of our persecution.
I will speak, even if I am not capable; I will recount, even if I cannot do it justice.
My soul is saddened because it cannot magnify the great deeds of these great men with praises of them.
My mind is distressed because it cannot glorify the glories of these glorious men with exaltations of them.
For look, their signs whisper to me in their wonder, and their miracles beckon to me in their marvel.
Look, their beauty gazes at me in its truth, and their splendor blossoms before me through their labors.
Look, their love makes me burn through its deeds, and their affection sets me ablaze through its vigils.
Look, their faith writes to me about them through its triumph, and there is drawn and portrayed for me concerning them
their endurance through its victory. Look, their slaughter prompts me to speak of them through its suffering, and their blood explains and instructs me about them through its sprinkling.
Look, their beloved memory makes my sins forgotten, and their cherished remembrance washes away my stains.
Look, they show my mind the champions of divinity and bring before my thoughts the mighty men of humanity.
They counsel me to recount their beauty [?], and urge me to speak of their glory as is fitting.
They command me to describe their race in its full measure, and urge me to make their toil known in its full extent.
Look, their spring has grown strong and abundant within my mind, but it has no broad outlet through my feeble [?].
Look, it has filled me and overflowed in its course, but my sealed lips will not open a channel for it.
Look, the pen disputes with me through its speech over writings that fall short of their [?],
and the scroll reproaches me through its silence over letters too small for their praises.
But let the reader consider with understanding, and let the listener comprehend with discernment:
although we have not composed praises worthy of them, we have written the truth about them as they were.
Their death is enough, and their slaughter suffices. For their death looks toward the death of the great, firmly fixed target. At him they aim and shoot; toward him
they draw their bows and take aim. Their bow is full of supplication and mercy; their arrow is anointed with suffering and tears.
They do not lodge their arrow in the target for their own glory, but for the praise of the one they gaze upon, they release and relax their right hands.
From him and toward him the shooter gains strength; he himself, through himself, directs the arm of the one who strikes.
Like him, the shooter is raised on a cross, for his own will has raised him on a cross like him, out of love for him.
And like him, the one who strikes is crucified, for his own freedom has crucified him like him, out of affection for him.
There are victory and a crown (for the archer [?]), who aims and sights with [?].
There are a reward and gifts for the trained man who skillfully takes aim and hits the mark.
There are lashes and disgrace for the boy who, through his carelessness, sent his arrow astray.
There are shame and rebuke for the fool who did not come forward to learn in the contests.
There the target stands upright and stretched out: the Crucified One, the lord of targets. There the [?] of the great martyr is poured out, the master of the [?] martyrs.
There is atonement for the sinner who brings his death to life through his death. There is forgiveness for the guilty man who atones for his blood through his blood.
There is recompense for the righteous man who glorifies his slaying through his slaying.
There the blood of many is poured out, of those who saw his blood pouring abundantly down the wood.
And those who longed for the slaying of their living Lord did not hold back from him when they themselves were slain. And those who joined their death to his death—he repays
them their lives through his life. O you who loved the Slain One with your blood, how eagerly his resurrection longs for your rising!
O you who loved the Crucified One through your slaying, how greatly his banquet rejoices in your delight!
He gave to you, and you gave to him, so that he might give to you and you might claim from him his sure promise in the kingdom.
As he said: “Whoever acknowledges me before people, I will acknowledge him before my Father in heaven and before his angels.”
Now the election of the blessed Mar Miles took place as follows.
He was from the country of the Raziqites, and in his youth he had been marked out to serve the earthly king.
But grace did not leave this wondrous vessel to remain there an earthly man like everyone else.
Instead, it led him to serve the heavenly King like a heavenly angel. He had approached baptism in faith.
And it was revealed to him in a vision by the Holy Spirit that on this path of discipleship to Christ he should remain a virgin.
Through constant fasting and frequent vigils, he weakened and wore down his body.
Through divine instruction he disciplined his soul and made it wise.
Through God's providence, a great door to new life had been opened to his mind.
The life-giving word was seething and overflowing in his heart,
and like a flame it burned and smoldered in his bones. And he could not bear to remain
in the place where he had become a disciple, because he was destined to benefit many.
So he left the city of Beth Lapat and went down to the city of Elam, where the citadel of Susa was.
And every day he taught and instructed its inhabitants with the word of truth and faithful preaching,
laboring and toiling for three years amid hardship and affliction.
There, through his love for the church of God, he advanced from rank to rank until he became a bishop,
through the laying on of hands by Gadiahb, bishop of the city of Beth Lapat,
who himself was also crowned with the noble martyrdom he suffered for Christ.
During these years when the blessed Miles was there and wore himself out,
that city was not persuaded at all to please God and find life. How often he persevered through his afflictions,
until they stoned him in its streets, dragged him away, and drove him out of it! Every day he received blows and endured them.
When he saw how firmly it clung to idolatry and the religion of the Magi, he left it and departed.
On the day he left it, he cursed it and said: “Because you were unwilling to be built up and perfected in peace,
may violent uprooting and swift destruction suddenly come upon you.
May your lofty buildings be torn down, and may your arrogant inhabitants be scattered.”
Three months after his departure, its leading men
—those of the city—offended the king. He sent three hundred elephants, and they overturned its dwellings and killed all its inhabitants.
They made it like an open plain and sowed it with mustard [that is, mustard;
and others read “fennel” [fennel? dill?], that is, [?]], down to the present day.
The holy man went to Jerusalem, carrying nothing with him except a Gospel book in a bag.
From there he went down to the city of Alexandria because of the reputation of the blessed Eunemius, a disciple of Anthony, the leader of the ascetics.
He stayed there for two years, visiting the brothers and their monasteries in the desert.
As he was returning to his own country, he found an ascetic living alone in a cave.
While the two of them were standing in prayer in the morning, a great snake called a Yawshpa suddenly appeared to them.
Its appearance was very hideous and terrifying, and it was thirty-two cubits long.
It began to enter the cave as usual, because it lived there.
But when the blessed Miles saw it, he was neither frightened nor shaken.
Instead, he took courage, stretched out his hand toward it, and said to it: “Bitter serpent and enemy of humanity,
“Why do you dare to drive us outside and go inside yourself? Look, even now the Lord’s spear
will split you from end to end as a miraculous sign.”
Immediately that snake swelled up all over and burst open from its head to its tail.
Then Miles asked that brother, “Had you seen this snake here before?” He answered him:
“It always lived in this cave. I too have been in it for some time, and it has not harmed me at all.”
But blessed Miles rebuked him severely and said to him:
“Since God, by his judicial decree, established hostility between human beings and the snake, why were you trusting an enemy
and sharing a dwelling with it?” Then he moved that brother from there to another place.
The blessed man continued his journey and came to the city of Nisibis.
He found a church being built by Bishop Jacob.
When he saw that the man was great and virtuous, and his [?] glorious and magnificent,
he stayed there a short time and then went down to Adiabene.
From there he sent him a bucketful of silk, no small amount, to cover the expenses of the building. Then he went down to Beth Aramaye.
He encountered a great dispute involving the bishop of Seleucia and Ctesiphon, who was called Papa bar Aggai.
He saw that Papa was exalting himself over the bishops of the regions who had gathered there for his trial,
and was also acting arrogantly toward the priests and deacons of his city.
He recognized the man’s arrogance toward them and the downfall that would come upon him from God. He stood up in their midst and said to him:
“Why do you act presumptuously and exalt yourself over your brothers and the members of your own body,
and envy them groundlessly and pointlessly, like a godless man? Is it not written:
‘Whoever is your leader must be your servant’?” Papa said to him:
“Are you teaching me these things, you fool? Surely I know them too!”
Immediately he approached, took the Gospel book from his bag, and placed it on a cushion before him. He said to him, “If from me,
from me personally, as a human being, you are unwilling to learn, then submit to judgment by our Lord’s Gospel,
which now lies before my outward eyes, since you do not see its commandment with the hidden eye of your mind.”
But Papa, in his wicked fury, raised his hand in anger and struck the Gospel book, saying, “Speak, Gospel, speak!”
Then the holy Miles was stirred, and he ran, took the Gospel book, kissed it, and placed it against his eyes.
And in a loud voice, within the hearing of that whole assembly: “Because in your arrogance you have dared to defy the living words of our Lord,
look, his angel is coming. He will strike you on one side of your body and wither it, and you will become an object of fear and terror to many.
You will not die immediately, but will remain as a sign and a wonder.” And immediately he came down from heaven like lightning,
struck him, and withered one side of his body. He lay on one side in indescribable torment for twelve years,
and died in this affliction. Fear and trembling came upon that whole assembly.
From there he went to the region of Maishan, to a certain hermit who lived in the wilderness.
It happened that the ruler of that region had been ill with a grievous disease for two years.
He heard that Miles had come there, and sent to ask him to come to him.
Then he said to the man who had brought the message, “Go, and when you enter, say in a loud voice, ‘Miles says:
In the name of Jesus of Nazareth, be healed; get up and walk.’” This was done in this way, and it was fully accomplished:
the man was healed, got up, and came to him. He and the inhabitants of that region praised God.
Many became disciples because of this sign. They also brought him a young man
who was subject to attacks by a spirit of epilepsy and had been tormented by it since childhood.
As soon as he saw him, he prayed and made the sign of the cross over him in the name of Jesus. That spirit departed from him and never attacked him again.
Many things like these were done through him in that region, to the glory of God.
From there he went to his own region, Beth Raziqaye.
He entered a village where there was a prominent woman
whose limbs had all been paralyzed by a severe illness for nine years.
Word spread about him and where he was staying. Her servants carried her and brought her to him there.
He looked at her and saw that she was distressed, for she was pleading earnestly with him.
Then he said to her, “Do you believe in the one God, who alone can heal you?” She said to him,
“I believe, my lord, that he alone is the one God, and there is no other besides him.”
Then he stood up and prayed, took her by the hand, and said to her, “In the name of the God in whom you have believed, get up and walk,
and be freed from your illness.” At that very moment the woman was healed of her illness.
She got up and went home, and there was joy throughout that village.
In that same village, two men came to him so that one might put the other under oath concerning the theft of something.
Miles said to the man who was to swear, “My son, do not swear falsely and wrong your companion in this whole affair.”
But he did not listen to him; he boldly swore the oath. Then the blessed man looked at him and said, “If you have sworn truthfully,
go home safe and sound. Otherwise, may Gehazi’s leprosy cover you, and may you depart in shame
from here.” Immediately that man became leprous all over.
Great fear came over that whole village, and many people there turned from paganism and became disciples.
He departed from there to go to another place, and two brothers went along to accompany him.
They came upon a large river, which detained them on its bank for a day because it could not be crossed on foot.
Then he appealed to those brothers, stood up and prayed, and dismissed them to return to their own place.
But they went only a little distance away from him and watched him to see what he would do or how he would cross.
He stood up and prayed, then walked over the river and crossed it without even taking his shoes off his feet.
He was welcomed in a village, where he found a deacon who was being accused of adultery.
He called him and rebuked him in the church itself, saying to him, “Confess, my son, if you are guilty of this,
and offer repentance to God, for he is merciful and will forgive you.
Do not dare, [?] you are not holy, to minister before him, [?] his justice suddenly destroys you.”
But that man brazenly said to him, “Oh, my lord, do not sin and speak
ill of me, for I have been falsely accused in this affair.”
Again he acted boldly, took the Book of David, and stood on the platform to chant.
Something like the palm of a hand came out of the sanctuary toward him and struck him in the face. Suddenly he fell down and died.
Great fear came over that whole region. In that same village they brought him a young man
who had crawled on his knees from birth because his feet and legs were twisted.
When he saw him, he stood up and prayed. He took him by the hand and said to him, “In the name of Jesus of Nazareth, get up and walk.”
Immediately his feet were released, his legs straightened, and he was healed. He got up and walked.
The young man who was healed was twenty years old.
As for the signs and great healings that were performed through him by the power [?] of God:
We could not write them all down, because they were so numerous.
But we now move briefly ahead to the great sign of his blood,
and to the extraordinary suffering of his death, and to his martyrdom, the glorious crown of his victories.
The ruler of that region, whose name was Hormizd Gufriz, had heard reports of his teaching.
He was wicked, conceited, arrogant, and boastful.
He sent for him, brought him to Mahledgard, the city of the Raziqites, and imprisoned him there
for some time, together with his two disciples, Abursam and Sinai.
Twice he tortured them with blows and lashes to make them worship the sun.
But they laughed at him a great deal and scorned his arrogance and his haughty treatment of them.
They stood firm in their truth and magnified the praise of their God in faith and truth.
When the year came around again, at the same time of year when he had imprisoned them, this wicked man was out hunting in the mountains.
His heart was full of joy in his pride. He gave an order, and they brought out all three holy men in their chains.
When they stood before him, he questioned the blessed Miles mockingly, saying to him:
“What are you? Are you a god or a human being? What is your faith, and what is your teaching? Show us your truth so that we may know it
and become your disciples. But if you are unwilling to reveal to us what you hold to,
I will take your head from you today, as I would from one of these animals.”
But the blessed man recognized the man's cunning and deceit, and said to him, “I am a human being, not a god.
I will not reveal my true faith to your deceitful falsehood, nor will I pour my pure teaching into your unclean ears.
But here is a straightforward word I will say to you: Woe to you! Woe to you,
you wicked evildoer, and to all those who, like you, live wickedly without God!
For in his justice God will judge you in the world to come, in Gehenna and the darkness that has been prepared,
and he will repay your arrogance with weeping and gnashing of teeth forever and ever,
because you have not recognized that it was he who gave you these good things in which you now take pride and indulge yourselves.”
Now this evildoer was sitting on a throne [?], and many people were standing before him.
When he heard these things, he became intensely enraged. He rose in his fury and drew the sword strapped to his thigh.
He struck Saint Miles in the shoulder from the front, and it came out through his back.
In this same wicked zeal, this wicked man's own brother, whose name was Narses,
also drew (his sword[?]) and struck him in the side, and it came out through his front.
Although the victorious martyr was already knocking at the gates of Sheol and, like an invited guest, was hastening to recline at death's banquet,
in his welcome death he prophesied about their dreadful death, speaking equally to both these brothers:
“Because you have so thoroughly agreed together in your wicked brotherhood and bound yourselves together in your bitter partnership to kill an innocent man and shed blood without cause,
look, tomorrow at this very time, your blood, together and by one another's hands,
will be shed in this place. Dogs will lick your blood, and the birds of the sky will eat your flesh.
Your mother will be bereaved of you both, and your wives will be widowed of you on a single day.”
When he had said these things, the saint's soul departed from him.
Then this wicked man gave orders concerning the victorious martyrs Abursam and Sinai, and they took them up onto two hills facing each other.
He sent many men from his army, and they stoned them there at the very time when blessed Miles was killed.
This Guphriz spent the night in that place.
When dawn came, a considerable number of wild animals were brought to him for the hunt.
His heart exalted him in his arrogance, and he was carried away. He disregarded the faithful man's words and put them out of his hearing.
At the very time when blessed Miles had been killed, the decree of the Most High overtook those warlike brothers,
who were trained in archery, skilled with the spear, practiced in bloodshed, and eager for the hunt.
For a doe broke through those linen barriers in which the wild animals were enclosed,
and swiftly escaped. Both reckless men rode after her, soon to die because they had killed so readily.
They positioned themselves, one on this side and one on the other, and both shot their arrows at the same moment,
intending, it seemed, to strike her skillfully from opposite sides.
Guphriz's arrow flew straight and passed through Narses's belly, while Narses's arrow
flew straight and went through Guphriz's chest. Both these archers fell
and died there, in the very place where blessed Miles had been killed.
They became a sight that caused amazement and news that caused terror throughout that whole country, and wild animals and birds ate their bodies.
For the Persians do not bury the dead until the flesh falls away from the bones, and then they conceal the bones themselves.
But that very night, people of the country stole the bodies of all three martyrs,
and took them away and buried them in a village called Malqin.
Thus, even in their death, a great miracle was revealed through them:
for raiders were constantly coming against that country to take captives and lay it waste.
Several times they reached the boundaries of that village but were stopped, and they did no harm there.
Its inhabitants believed that it was because of the blessing of the bones of the righteous buried within it that the raiders had not been allowed to enter.
The saints were crowned on the thirteenth of the latter Tishrin [?], according to the lunar calendar.
